idiom_name: sealed message hierarchy + exhaustive when, rule table published through a MutableStateFlow
implementation_notes: Kotlin's realization splits into a closed part and an open part: the message shape is a sealed hierarchy handled by an exhaustive when (no else clause, so adding a message type is a compile error), while the runtime-editable part - which destination currently serves a key - lives in a MutableStateFlow<Map<String, Handler>> whose value is read once per message; StateFlow reads are thread-safe and always see the newest published value. Rule updates are published with update {} from a control coroutine, and because StateFlow conflates on equality, publishing the same table twice is a no-op rather than a re-emit. Where the key set is genuinely open, use a plain Map registry instead of adding cases to the sealed hierarchy.
pitfalls: MutableStateFlow conflates on equals: publishing a table equal to the current one emits nothing, which is correct for routing but hides a no-op update from observers and metrics.
update {} retries under contention, so do not build the replacement table inside the lambda - construct it first, then call update.
A suspend handler must not block a dispatcher thread; a blocking destination call needs its own dispatcher (or the handler turns the router into a bottleneck).
Capturing the routing table in a long-lived coroutine pins the old rule objects and their captured resources.
